title: TOWER-hard reachability with seven nonnegative counters
formal: Is reachability in unary-encoded seven-dimensional vector addition systems with states (7-VASS) \(\mathrm{TOWER}\)-hard under elementary-time many-one reductions?
why: This seeks the dimension at which a small collection of nonnegative counters can already encode nonelementary computational difficulty. Reducing the eight-counter frontier would sharpen the low-dimensional boundary between tractable geometric behavior and extreme reachability complexity.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The 2025 question and LICS 2026 paper retain eight as the known ordinary-VASS TOWER-hard dimension. The latter’s hardness with three nonnegative counters also uses signed counters and does not settle the present target. No seven-counter resolution was located in the bounded subsequent-work check.

progress.text: Czerwiński and Orlikowski establish TOWER-hardness for unary 8-VASS.
Orlikowski asks whether the eight-counter TOWER lower bound can be achieved in smaller dimension.
The LICS 2026 signed-counter extension still identifies dimension eight as the ordinary-VASS TOWER-hardness frontier; its smaller-dimensional result uses extra signed counters.

sentences: A VASS combines finite control with nonnegative integer counters updated by fixed transition vectors.
The question asks for TOWER-hard reachability using only seven counters and unary-encoded numbers.
Seven counters capture the source’s request for any improvement below the known eight-counter bound, by padding unused coordinates.
TOWER-hardness uses elementary-time reductions and is stronger than a collection of unrelated fixed-height exponential lower bounds.
Recent lower bounds with extra signed counters concern a different computational model.

definitions: A \(d\)-VASS has a finite nonempty control-state set \(Q\) and a finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\mathbb Z^d\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,x)\in Q\times\mathbb N^d\), where \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q^{\prime})\) takes \((q,x)\) to \((q^{\prime},x+a)\) exactly when every coordinate of \(x+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests, counter resets, unrestricted signed counters, stacks or fractional updates. An instance gives \(Q,E\) and source and target configurations; reachability asks for a finite transition sequence between them, possibly of length zero. For the target \(d=7\) is fixed, but the control graph, vectors and endpoint configurations are inputs. They are listed explicitly. Every integer magnitude in a displacement or endpoint is unary, with a separate sign where necessary; state identifiers use a finite binary encoding. Let \(e_0(n)=n\) and \(e_{j+1}(n)=2^{e_j(n)}\). An elementary time bound is bounded by \(e_k(n^c+c)\) for fixed nonnegative integer \(k\) and positive integer \(c\). Define \(T(0)=1\), \(T(h+1)=2^{T(h)}\). The class \(\mathrm{TOWER}\) consists of languages decidable by deterministic Turing machines in time \(O(T(f(n)))\) for some elementary-time computable nonnegative integer function \(f\). A many-one reduction from a binary language \(K\) to VASS reachability is a total computable function mapping each input string to a valid VASS instance, preserving yes and no answers. Elementary-time reductions must obey one elementary time bound for each fixed source language. TOWER-hardness quantifies over every language in TOWER; it does not additionally assert that the target problem belongs to TOWER.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of TOWER-hardness in exactly the stated seven-counter, unary-encoded model and reduction convention. Alternatively prove in Lean that this problem is not TOWER-hard under those reductions. An elementary algorithm would imply a negative answer, but the target does not require that stronger conclusion. Results using eight counters or additional signed counters do not establish the required lower bound.

context_blocks.text: The original 2025 question asks whether the known eight-counter hardness can be attained in a lower dimension. This is exactly captured by testing seven counters: a lower-dimensional VASS can be padded with permanently zero counters, without changing reachability.

Czerwiński and Orlikowski prove TOWER-hardness already with eight counters and unary displacement encoding. Their result therefore cannot be explained solely by exponentially succinct binary counter values. The elementary reduction convention is significant for this nonelementary complexity class.

A fixed-height tower, such as a double or triple exponential, is an elementary bound. TOWER allows the tower height itself to grow with the input. Hardness for every fixed-height exponential class does not on its own supply the single TOWER-hardness statement.

The 2026 work on VASS extended with signed integer counters reports the ordinary three-counter reachability problem as elementary and the ordinary TOWER lower bound as known in dimension eight. Its new three-counter hardness counts only the nonnegative counters and permits additional unrestricted integer counters. Those extra counters are absent from the present model.

The number of counters stays fixed but the finite control graph can grow. This differs from fixing the entire VASS and varying only its endpoints. It also differs from requiring a long run in a particular example: a complexity lower bound must reduce every problem in the hardness class.

The source separately discusses geometric dimension, defined using the span of cycle effects. That structural parameter is not substituted for the seven actual nonnegative counters in this card; its associated question remains a distinct direction.
